transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Thanks for seeing me, I really appreciate it. Um... I guess what brings me in is... well, it's a little embarrassing, to be honest. I didn't mean to cause any trouble, but I had a bit of a moment at work. 

I'm a personal care aide, and I just try really hard to do a good job, you know? We were in a staff meeting, and I guess I just got a little too worked up about safety. I started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of everything. I was moving chairs around and waving my arms to show how someone might slip... and, well, some folks told me to sit down and take it easy. 

The thing is, I... I just couldn't seem to stop. Even when they asked me to. I was just so focused on showing them, I guess? I hope that doesn't sound too bad. I really just wanted to be helpful and make sure everyone was safe. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it okay.
In the days leading up to and including that incident, did you notice yourself feeling unusually energetic, upbeat, or needing much less sleep than normal?

Um... well, I guess I was feeling pretty good? Like, really productive. I hope it's okay to say that. As for sleep, um... I really didn't seem to need much, but I felt completely fine! 

I'd been sleeping maybe two or three hours, tops. But I'd wake up way before dawn and just feel... totally rested and ready to go. I honestly didn't think anything was wrong with it at all. I'd just be up, making all these plans for work and getting things organized while the house was still pitch dark. I figured I was just being a go-getter and getting a good head start on the day, you know? 

Is... is that the kind of thing you mean? I hope that doesn't mean I was doing something wrong.
How many days in a row have you been feeling this unusually energetic and needing so little sleep?

Well, um... I guess it hasn't just been a few days. I hope that's alright to admit. 

It's actually been kind of... coming and going for a while now. Like, maybe around 11 months or so? There will be these stretches where I'm just super energized, barely sleeping, and coming up with all these big plans for work and stuff. And then it kind of settles down, but it always comes back. 

I really didn't think it was a big deal, honestly. I just thought I was going through phases of being really motivated, you know? I hope I haven't been letting this go on for too long without saying something. Is it... is it bad that it's been happening for almost a year?
When you're in one of these energized, low-sleep phases, how many days in a row does it usually last before it settles down?

Um... gosh, I'm not exactly sure about the exact number of days. I hope it's okay that I haven't kept a strict count. 

I guess... well, I haven't really paid that much attention to how long each stretch lasts. It just sort of happens and then it passes. I try to just focus on doing a good job when I have all that energy, you know? 

I'm sorry I don't have a better answer for you. Does that make sense, though? Like, not really tracking it because it just felt like I was being productive? I hope that's an okay answer.
Aside from these energized stretches, have you also had separate periods—lasting days or weeks—where you felt unusually down, low on energy, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I hope it's okay to say that, but I don't think I've had anything like that. 

I try to keep a pretty positive attitude, you know? Especially with my job, helping people... I try to stay upbeat for them. So I haven't really had any long stretches of feeling super down or anything. Sometimes I get a little tired, but I think that's just normal, right? 

I really try not to let myself get too low. Is... is that a good thing? I hope I'm answering this the right way. I just haven't really noticed any big periods of feeling depressed or anything like that.
During that episode at work, did your coworkers or supervisors take any action—like sending you home, disciplining you, or requiring you to see someone—because your behavior was so disruptive?

Well, um... I guess they did have to do something. I hope you don't think less of me for this. 

They... they put me on leave from the senior center. I think they just wanted to make sure I was okay, you know? It wasn't like a punishment, I don't think. I just wasn't keeping up with things the way I usually do. 

Even at home, my wife has had to remind me to do my chores and keep track of my appointments. I feel terrible about it, honestly. I've always tried to be so reliable. I've even pulled back from my friends at church because I just... I don't want them to see me like this. 

And now I'm just worrying if I can even go back to my caregiving work safely. I want to, I really do. I love helping people. I just hope I haven't messed everything up. Is it... is it normal to struggle this much with keeping up with things? I really want to get back to being myself again.

During these high-energy periods, have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things others don't see, or having beliefs—like feeling you had special powers or a special mission—that others told you weren't true?

Um... well... I guess maybe a little bit? I really hope you don't think I'm crazy or anything for saying this. 

When I was in those really fired-up stretches, you know, when I was only sleeping a few hours and trying to get all those big plans going... sometimes I thought I heard people calling out to me, but there wasn't anyone there. I tried to just ignore it, though. 

And... well, I also got it into my head that my supervisor was setting traps for me at work. I know that probably sounds bad, and I feel kind of embarrassed admitting it now. I didn't want to cause any trouble, I just... I felt so sure about it at the time. 

Is it okay that I'm telling you this? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information so I can get better and go back to helping people. I'm not a bad person, I promise.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes a manic episode with markedly elevated, goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours with no fatigue), pressured/expansive behavior severe enough to disrupt a work meeting and result in administrative leave, along with impaired occupational and social functioning (withdrawal from church, needing spousal reminders for basic tasks). During this high-energy period, the patient also endorsed psychotic features—auditory hallucinations (hearing voices calling out) and paranoid/persecutory delusions (belief that a supervisor was 'setting traps'). These mood-congruent psychotic symptoms occurred exclusively during the manic phase, not persisting outside of it, and there is no history of a distinct major depressive episode, ruling out classic bipolar I without current psychotic mania (F31.1) and schizoaffective disorder (F25.0). The overall pattern—recurrent hypomanic/manic-like phases over ~11 months culminating in a severe manic episode with psychotic features—supports Bipolar I Disorder, current episode manic, severe, with psychotic symptoms (F31.2). Major depressive disorder with psychosis (F30.2 as unipolar mania alternative was considered but excluded since this represents a bipolar course, and F32.3 excluded since there is no depressive episode).
